title: Rubber stamp
suits: compliance, legal, logistics, customs, government, approvals: anything with forms, sign-off and a paper trail

params.--field: the paper (manila by default; any colour or gradient)
params.--brand: the ink, used if it reads on the field (3.2:1)
params.--brand-2: fallback ink; if neither reads, the engine's readable ink tinted toward the brand
params.--stamp-wood / --stamp-rail: the beech block and the walnut rail
params.--stamp-fs: wordmark size (long names shrink the die to fit 1560 px)
params.--stamp-case: uppercase by default; none keeps the brand's own casing
params.--stamp-tilt: how far off square the hand put it (-1.6deg)
params.__MARK__: stroke paths in a 24 x 24 box, inked as thick round strokes; the block label copies it

details: the block falls with gravity (accelerating) and turns from 8.5° to its final 1.6° as it is placed
two shadows: a soft one that trails far off while the block is high, a crisp contact shadow that appears only as it lands
the whole field nudges 1 px down on impact and recoils 0.4 px
the rubber squashes on contact (wider, shorter) and springs back a beat before the block leaves the paper
the hand rocks the block a hair while pressing, so the right side of the impression inks lighter
the index label on top of the block carries a tiny print of the impression, as real stamps do
ink pools at the edges of every glyph (darker rims, lighter mottled body)
rough, fibrous edges and starved pinholes from the paper texture
ink speckles thrown from the die edge, two larger splats at opposite corners
a faint broken ring where the block edge kissed the paper
the ink lands wet (darker) and dries matte over a second
the impression sits 1.6° off square, like a human hand put it there
manila fibre and slow blotches in the field; the block has real end-grain from noise
the wet ink is the dry ink pushed further from the paper (darker on light paper, brighter on dark paper)
the label's tiny print falls back to near-black when the ink would not read on the cream label
